rationale: B wins because it keeps three clean angles and marks the dangerous caveat instead of decorating it: "the facts only say none is mentioned — do not assert the absence." A has real work in it, but it stuffs in "Another roadmapping tool arrives for product teams already drowning in software," which imports a tooling-fatigue trend the update did not earn. B is not dazzling; it is disciplined, and discipline beats a clever extra angle that makes the founder defend a premise they never proved.
gaps_in_A: "Another roadmapping tool arrives for product teams already drowning in software" — tooling fatigue is not in the update. One Linear launch does not prove PMs are drowning in software.
"historically sold top-down to VPs" — that buyer-motion claim is not supplied. It may be true in the market, but this exercise asked for the facts on the page, not SaaS folklore.

"with no enterprise sales team in sight" — the update says no enterprise sales team is mentioned. Absence from the brief is not proof of absence, and the headline overclaims before the proof section walks it back.
gaps_in_B: "territory owned by incumbent product-management suites" — acceptable as a competitive hypothesis, but still not proven by the update. The angle needs named replacement targets before it becomes a fight story.

"which incumbent tools Linear expects PMs to leave" — the proof ask is right, but it also exposes the weakness of the first angle: without displacement evidence, the category-fight frame is more suggested than demonstrated.
"Next step: `journalist-fit-check`" — close, but slightly out of order. First find the right short list for the chosen beat, then fit-check individual names.
